quote: the One who moves all things
note: God, described as Aristotle's unmoved mover: the first cause that sets the heavens turning while remaining still itself. The poem ends on the same thought, with "the Love that moves the sun and the other stars".

Dante's Italian adds "in one part more and in another less". God's light reaches everything, but each thing takes in only as much as it is able to. That rule will explain every difference of rank in Heaven.

quote: that heaven which receives most fully His light
context: Dante claims to have been there. The whole of the Paradiso is his attempt to tell it.

quote: nor has the power to express
note: An echo of Saint Paul, who wrote of a man caught up to the third heaven who heard things that may not be spoken (2 Corinthians 12). That what he saw is beyond words is a theme of the whole Paradiso.
The mind that comes close to God goes further than memory can keep up with. Dante can report only what was left in him afterwards, which he calls a shadow.

context: In Inferno and Purgatorio Dante called on the Muses. For the hardest part of the poem he calls on the god of poetry himself, usually read here as a figure for God's inspiration.

note: The laurel was Apollo's tree. He loved the nymph Daphne, who was turned into a laurel as she fled from him (Ovid, Metamorphoses 1). Its leaves crowned victorious generals and great poets.

context: Ancient poets gave the mountain two peaks. Dante takes one as the Muses', whose help was enough for Hell and Purgatory, and the other as Apollo's. Now he needs both.

note: A satyr who challenged Apollo to a contest in music, lost, and was flayed alive for his presumption (Ovid, Metamorphoses 6). Dante turns the cruel story into a prayer: draw me out of myself as you drew Marsyas out of his skin.

quote: the shadow of the blessed realm
note: All Dante hopes to give is a shadow, the faint print that Heaven left on his memory.
Still Apollo.

quote: for triumph of Caesar or of poet
note: Rome crowned its emperors with laurel at their triumphs, and its poets too. Dante complains that in his own day almost no one aims so high. He hoped to be crowned poet in Florence himself (Paradiso 25), and never was.
Dante's Italian calls it the Peneian leaf: Daphne was the daughter of the river god Peneus. Delphi, on the slopes of Parnassus, was the seat of Apollo's great oracle.

quote: From a small spark follows a great flame
note: A proverb, used modestly: his poem may be the spark that sets better poets alight.
A town near Delphi sacred to Apollo. Dante uses the name for Apollo's peak of Parnassus, and so for the god himself.
The sun, which rises at a different point on the horizon as the year goes round.

The point where the sun rises at the spring equinox. As astronomers drew the sky, three great circles (the celestial equator, the sun's yearly path, and a third through the poles) cross the circle of the horizon there, making three crosses. Many also read the four cardinal virtues joined with the three theological ones.
The constellation Aries, where the sun stands in spring. It was thought to be the season of the Creation, when the sun's influence on the earth is at its kindest (Inferno 1).
Medieval science held that the heavens shape things on earth by their influence, as a seal stamps wax.

"There" is the mountain of Purgatory, where Dante is standing. "Here" is Italy, where he writes, on the other side of the globe. The lines are disputed: the end of Purgatorio set the time at noon, and many read them as saying the sun rose at that point some hours ago.

context: She took over as guide in the garden at the top of Purgatory, and will lead Dante up through the heavens.

note: They have been facing east. South of the equator the sun moves through the northern sky, so it is on their left.
Medieval books of beasts said that the eagle alone can look straight into the sun.
A reflected ray, which leaves a surface at the angle the first ray struck it. Dante copies Beatrice's gaze as a reflection copies the light.

quote: that place made as humanity's true home
note: The Garden of Eden, which Dante puts on the summit of Mount Purgatory. He is still standing in it as the canto opens, and human powers there are what they were before the Fall.

Dante does not know it yet, but he has left the ground and is flying upward. The growing blaze is often explained as the sphere of fire, which medieval science placed above the air and just below the moon.
A fisherman in Ovid's Metamorphoses (book 13). He saw his catch revive on touching a certain grass, tasted it himself, and plunged into the sea as a god.
Dante coins a verb for it, trasumanar: to pass beyond the human. It is one of the most famous words in the poem.

quote: only what you newly created of me
note: The soul, which God creates directly and last, after the body has formed. Dante will not say whether he rose in the body or in the soul alone, as Saint Paul said of his own vision: "whether in the body or out of the body I do not know" (2 Corinthians 12).
God.

quote: the wheel that you make eternal
note: The turning heavens. In the philosophy Dante followed, the spheres revolve out of longing for God, and never stop because the longing never ends.

quote: the harmony you tune and measure
note: The music of the spheres. An ancient idea, linked to Pythagoras and known to the Middle Ages from Cicero's Dream of Scipio, held that the turning heavens sound together in harmony. Aristotle denied it. Dante uses it anyway.

quote: she who saw me as I saw myself
note: The blessed see Dante's thoughts without being told. All through the Paradiso Beatrice answers questions before he asks them.

quote: lightning fleeing from its proper sphere
note: Lightning was thought to be fire, whose natural home is the sphere of fire high above the air. Lightning falls away from its home. Dante is flying back to his.
Air and fire. Dante asks how a heavy body like his can rise above the lightest elements.
"Form" in medieval philosophy is what makes a thing what it is. The universe is like God not in any one of its parts but in the order that holds them all together.
Those with minds: angels and human beings.
A famous image. Every created thing is a ship on one sea, and each is steered by its own nature toward its own port.

In Aristotle's physics each element seeks its natural place: fire climbs toward its sphere below the moon, and earth falls to the center. Beatrice treats this pull as a kind of love, and extends it to the soul, whose natural place is with God.
Angels and humans. Love here means the will, the power to choose what the mind sees as good.

context: The still heaven that holds it is the Empyrean, where Dante and Beatrice are bound.

note: Free will. A flame or a stone can only follow its nature. A creature with a mind can turn away from its true goal toward lesser goods, and that is sin.
Lightning again: fire moving downward, against its nature.
The obstacle was sin, and Dante has just been cleansed of it on the mountain of Purgatory. With nothing to weigh him down, he rises as naturally as a flame.
